blocks.text: At a fixed i, one history permits choosing nums[i] and another forbids it. Those histories cannot share one cached result unless the state records that distinction. The accumulated score is usually added outside the suffix value rather than used as identity, because it does not change the suffix choices. A sufficient state is the smallest summary that makes all histories mapped to it future-equivalent.

messages.text: The same i can be reached with different legality for choosing i, so index alone merges states with different future options.
The accumulated sum does not identify which positions remain or whether the current position is legal; it omits future-relevant information.

blocks.text: Two calls at item i with capacities 3 and 10 do not ask the same question: the latter may take items the former cannot. Caching both under i would allow a result computed for one feasible set to contaminate the other. An index-only state is not inherently wrong; it is wrong here because it fails the future-equivalence test. Start from the state meaning, then include exactly the variables that change the unresolved problem.

messages.text: Index-only state is valid when the index fully determines the remaining choices, as in many prefix or suffix recurrences without another resource.
Dimensionality is determined by information sufficiency, not a blanket performance rule; extra dimensions generally increase state count.

constraints: The unresolved suffixes are first[i:] and second[j:].

blocks.text: A memo key is the operational representation of the DP state. If the recurrence meaning depends on (i, j), the cache must distinguish every reachable pair unless a proven invariant derives one coordinate from the other. Faster lookup cannot compensate for false equivalence. Fix the state/key first; only then compare top-down and bottom-up cost.

messages.text: A missing base case would be separate; even with perfect bases, the index-only key still aliases distinct suffix pairs.
The defect is semantic, not a universal performance claim; a correctly keyed memo can remove substantial recomputation.

blocks.text: dp(r, c) still denotes a result for a particular row and column. During row-by-row evaluation, the current iteration variable supplies r, while the array retains only values that remain live. This is a storage optimization, not a redefinition of the subproblem. If dependencies or reconstruction need discarded rows, the compression is invalid even though the logical state remains well-defined.

messages.text: Some recurrences read multiple older rows, arbitrary cells, or require the full table for reconstruction.
The value at column c still has different meanings for different rows; the row is implicit in the evaluation phase, not absent from the semantic state.

constraints: Past score does not change which future choices are legal.

blocks.text: For a fixed i, the set of remaining choices and the maximum additional score are identical across all past totals. The caller can add the already-earned amount outside the memoized function. Including it would fragment one reusable state into many copies and may eliminate overlap. The boundary changes if the accumulated value affects legality, a target, or a future reward.

messages.text: Only future-relevant information belongs in the key. Including an irrelevant accumulator can multiply states without changing the suffix answer.
Different histories may safely merge when the state contract deliberately removes history that has no effect on the future.

constraints: A transition may advance i, j, or both.

blocks.text: A state must distinguish every combination of remaining suffixes that can lead to a different answer. Because a transition can skip in either string, multiple j values are reachable at one i and vice versa. Storing only one coordinate would merge different alignment problems. This is the same sufficiency test used for grid rows and columns: include each independent axis of future behavior.

messages.text: The two suffixes can advance independently, so the same i can pair with many j values and different remaining matches.

blocks.text: Two calls with the same index but different capacities can admit different future selections, so they cannot share one answer. blocks.text: Memoization is sound when the state definition captures every future-relevant fact. Histories that differ only in irrelevant past detail can merge; histories with different remaining inputs or constraints must remain distinct. Reuse means compute the recurrence once, not skip the recurrence or erase its constraints.

messages.text: The first arrival does not determine the optimal subproblem value; the recurrence still must be evaluated.
Constraints are part of the state precisely because they affect future transitions.
Separating equivalent states forfeits the repeated-subproblem benefit without improving correctness.

feedback.reason: State equivalence is precisely the condition that lets dynamic programming share a subproblem answer across histories.

options.text: Reuse one computed answer for both histories because their future subproblem is identical.

Discard the future constraints because memoization makes them redundant.

blocks.text: If every cell reads only the previous row and current-row left value, two rows can preserve those dependencies. Overwriting a value before its last read changes the recurrence, even when the asymptotic space looks attractive. Compression must implement the same state semantics, not redefine the answer.

messages.text: An optimization must preserve the original recurrence and output contract.
